Neurology · published research

Brain circulation

Acute near-infrared stimulation increased oxygenated and reduced deoxygenated hemoglobin in healthy volunteers. Repeated treatment also reduced task-related cortical activation in one older-adult study, so the direction depends on the measure and setting.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Acute near-infrared stimulation increased oxygenated and reduced deoxygenated hemoglobin in healthy volunteers. Repeated treatment also reduced task-related cortical activation in one older-adult study, so the direction depends on the measure and setting.

Summary of the Evidence

Seven unique publications appear in the direct brain-circulation category: four human reports and three rat experiments. The human studies comprise two single-session or repeated physiology experiments, one single-arm study in older women, and one case report. The two acute experiments in the Tian paper are separate experimental conditions within one publication, not two independent article records. A mouse study of carotid-stenosis hypoperfusion is in a neighboring category and is not included in the direct count.

Human and clinical evidence

Tian et al. conducted two acute experiments in healthy adults using 1064 nm near-infrared laser light on the forehead. During ten minutes of stimulation, oxygenated hemoglobin increased and deoxygenated hemoglobin decreased in both hemispheres. The oxygenation response grew over the exposure and remained measurable during a six-minute recovery period. These are direct physiologic measurements, not evidence that a vascular disease improved (Tian et al. 2016).

In 61 healthy older adults, one week of daily 1064 nm PBM was followed by lower bilateral cortical hemodynamic activation during a working-memory task compared with the baseline sham visit. A smaller task-related response is not automatically better or worse; the study measured brain activation, not stroke risk or clinical circulation (Hu et al. 2023).

A single-arm study of 25 older women used transcranial red LED treatment and transcranial Doppler to assess cerebral blood flow. The paper reports blood-flow measurements before and after treatment, but the database flags a discrepancy in the reported number of sessions between the abstract and full text. A separate case report measured regional cerebral oxygenation and temperature after an 810 nm LED-array treatment (Salgado et al. 2015 Litscher et al., 2019).

Animal evidence

Three rat publications examine pial arteries or brain capillaries. They use 473 nm blue visible light, 633 or 650 nm red visible light, and differing exposure levels. Outcomes include vessel reactivity and capillary responses; one report describes a biphasic response, meaning the measured effect differed across exposure levels. These experiments are not clinical studies of circulation disorders.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell or ex-vivo study is classified in the direct brain-circulation category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Human protocols include 1064 nm near-infrared laser light for ten minutes or 12 minutes daily for seven days, 627 nm red visible LED treatment in older women, and an 810 nm near-infrared LED array in a case report. The rat work includes blue and red visible wavelengths. Session schedules, dose reporting, and measured outcomes differ. There is no head-to-head dose study, and a short-lived oxygenation change cannot be assumed to improve clinical circulation.

Interpretation

The acute healthy-volunteer experiments show that forehead near-infrared stimulation can increase oxygenated hemoglobin and lower deoxygenated hemoglobin during and shortly after exposure. Other measures, such as task-related cortical activation, moved in a different direction after repeated treatment. These findings establish physiologic responses under specific conditions, while treatment benefit for stroke or other vascular disease remains untested.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for acute cerebral oxygenation responses in healthy adults No clinical evidence for treatment of cerebrovascular disease
Publications and records7 unique publications

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Human experiments report immediate changes in cerebral oxygenation, while other studies measure task-related cortical activation or blood-flow measures without a disease-treatment comparison. The acute physiologic response is measurable, but it is not itself proof of improved symptoms or prevention of stroke. Controlled studies that link repeatable perfusion changes to function in a defined patient group would support a stronger clinical rating.
